questions.stem: A patient with short limbs, a normal-sized trunk, and a large head relative to the limbs is found to have a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3. Which process is most directly impaired?
explanations: Correct: achondroplasia is caused by an activating (gain-of-function) FGFR3 mutation that inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, impairing endochondral ossification (longitudinal bone growth from cartilage), resulting in short limbs; membranous ossification is unaffected, so head size is relatively preserved/large.
Membranous ossification (formation of flat bones like the skull) is not affected in achondroplasia, which is why the skull develops normally while limbs are short.
Vitamin D activation defects cause rickets/osteomalacia, not achondroplasia.
Osteoclast differentiation defects cause osteopetrosis, not achondroplasia.
questions.overview: Achondroplasia, the most common cause of dwarfism, is caused by an autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 that inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, impairing endochondral ossification and causing short limbs with a normal trunk and relatively large head. Membranous ossification is unaffected, and most cases arise from spontaneous mutation associated with increased paternal age; homozygous mutations are lethal.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old soccer player plants her foot and suddenly changes direction, feeling a "pop" in her knee followed by swelling. With the knee flexed to 30 degrees, the tibia translates further anteriorly than normal compared with the contralateral side. Which structure is most likely injured?
explanations: MCL injury results from valgus stress and shows abnormal passive abduction/medial joint space widening, not increased anterior tibial translation.

Correct: noncontact pivoting injuries with a "pop" and effusion are classic for ACL tears; the Lachman test (anterior translation at 30 degrees) demonstrating excessive anterior tibial movement confirms ACL insufficiency, since the ACL normally resists anterior tibial movement.
LCL injury results from varus stress and shows abnormal passive adduction/lateral joint space widening, not increased anterior tibial translation.
Meniscal tears present with pain/pop on twisting and a positive McMurray test, not increased anterior tibial translation.
PCL injury is typically caused by a posteriorly directed force (dashboard injury) and shows a positive posterior drawer sign, not increased anterior translation.
questions.overview: The ACL is the most commonly injured knee ligament, classically torn during noncontact pivoting/cutting movements with a sensation of a "pop," and it resists anterior tibial translation. The Lachman test (30° flexion) is more sensitive than the anterior drawer test (90° flexion) for detecting ACL laxity.

questions.stem: A patient with an anomalous extra rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra develops arm pain and paresthesias that worsen with arm elevation, along with intermittent hand swelling. Which condition is most likely?
explanations: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from median nerve compression at the wrist, unrelated to a cervical rib or symptoms worsened by arm elevation.
Guyon canal syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression at the wrist, not related to a cervical rib.

Correct: a cervical rib is a classic cause of thoracic outlet syndrome, compressing the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels; symptoms worsen with arm elevation and can include venous compression (swelling) or arterial compression.
Cubital tunnel syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, not related to a cervical rib.
questions.overview: Thoracic outlet syndrome results from compression of the lower brachial plexus trunk and subclavian vessels as they exit the thorax, often due to a cervical rib, scalene muscle hypertrophy, or compression beneath the pectoralis minor. Symptoms (Klumpke-pattern weakness, paresthesias) worsen with arm elevation, and venous or arterial compression can cause swelling or ischemic symptoms, respectively.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the mechanism of smooth muscle contraction following calcium entry into the cell?
options: Calcium activates myosin light chain phosphatase, phosphorylating myosin
Calcium directly binds myosin heavy chain to initiate the power stroke
Calcium binds troponin C, removing tropomyosin's inhibitory block on actin
Calcium binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates myosin light chain to permit actin-myosin interaction
explanations: Myosin light chain phosphatase dephosphorylates (not phosphorylates) myosin and promotes relaxation, not contraction.
Calcium does not directly bind myosin heavy chain; it acts via calmodulin/MLCK to phosphorylate the myosin light chain.
Calcium binding troponin C to remove tropomyosin's block is the mechanism of skeletal/cardiac (striated) muscle contraction ("thin filament regulated"), not smooth muscle, which lacks troponin.

Correct: in smooth muscle, calcium binds calmodulin, and the calcium-calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the myosin light chain, allowing myosin to interact with actin ("thick filament regulated"); dephosphorylation by myosin light chain phosphatase promotes relaxation.
questions.overview: Unlike striated muscle (which is "thin filament regulated" via troponin/tropomyosin), smooth muscle contraction is "thick filament regulated": calcium binds calmodulin, and the calcium-calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates myosin light chains to enable actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling. Myosin light chain phosphatase reverses this phosphorylation, promoting relaxation; second messengers (cAMP inhibits MLCK, cGMP activates the phosphatase) further modulate tone.

questions.stem: A patient develops fever, muscle rigidity, and markedly elevated creatine kinase shortly after receiving succinylcholine and halothane during surgery. Which drug is the appropriate treatment, and what is its mechanism?
options: Verapamil; blocks L-type calcium channels on the sarcolemma
Calcium gluconate; replaces depleted calcium stores
Dantrolene; blocks ryanodine receptor-mediated calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
explanations: Verapamil blocks L-type calcium channels on the cell surface, not the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is the actual defect in malignant hyperthermia.
Calcium gluconate would worsen the condition, which is driven by excessive calcium release, not calcium deficiency.
Epinephrine would not address the underlying excessive calcium release and is not the treatment for malignant hyperthermia.

Correct: malignant hyperthermia results from abnormal ryanodine receptors causing excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in response to certain anesthetics (halothane, succinylcholine), leading to sustained contraction, heat generation, and muscle damage; dantrolene antagonizes the ryanodine receptor, blocking calcium release and treating the condition.
questions.overview: Malignant hyperthermia is a rare, dangerous reaction to certain anesthetics (halothane, succinylcholine) caused by abnormal ryanodine receptors that trigger excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to sustained muscle contraction, heat production, rigidity, elevated CK, and hyperkalemia. Treatment is dantrolene, which blocks the ryanodine receptor and halts calcium release.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand and sustains an anterior dislocation of the humeral head. After closed reduction, she has weakness with abduction of the arm beyond 15 degrees and decreased sensation over the lateral shoulder ("deltoid patch"). Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanations: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus/infraspinatus (initial abduction 0°-15°, external rotation), not the 15°-90° abduction or deltoid patch sensation described here.
Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior arm/dorsal hand, not deltoid weakness; it is classically injured by midshaft humerus fracture, not shoulder dislocation.

Correct: the axillary nerve (C5-C6) runs below the humeral head/surgical neck, innervates the deltoid (abduction 15°-90°) and provides sensation to the deltoid patch; it is classically injured in anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humerus fracture.
Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula from serratus anterior weakness, unrelated to this presentation.
Musculocutaneous nerve injury causes weak elbow flexion/supination and lateral forearm sensory loss, not deltoid weakness or the sensory pattern described.
questions.overview: The axillary nerve (C5-C6) arises from the posterior cord, wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus, and innervates the deltoid (abduction 15°-90°) and teres minor, with sensory supply to the "deltoid patch." It is classically injured by anterior shoulder dislocation or proximal humerus fracture, producing a flattened deltoid and loss of abduction beyond 15°.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is found to have an isolated elevation in serum alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH. Imaging shows a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with irregular cement lines. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes elevated calcium and PTH with low phosphate, not normal calcium/PTH.
Osteomalacia is associated with elevated PTH and low calcium/phosphate/vitamin D, not normal labs with isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation.

Correct: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of excessive, disorganized bone remodeling (increased osteoclastic then osteoblastic activity) occurring in older patients, producing an isolated elevation in alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium/phosphate/PTH, and a characteristic mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with irregular cement lines on histology.
Osteopetrosis is due to defective osteoclast activity causing increased bone density, not the mosaic pattern/cement lines described; alkaline phosphatase elevation is not the classic finding.
questions.overview: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of excessive bone remodeling, evolving through osteolytic, mixed, and osteosclerotic phases, that produces disorganized, enlarged bone with a characteristic "mosaic pattern" of lamellar bone and irregular cement lines. Labs show an isolated elevation in alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH; complications include fractures, hearing loss, high-output heart failure, and increased osteosarcoma risk.

questions.stem: A breastfed infant with limited sun exposure develops bowed legs, widened wrists, and a "rachitic rosary." Which of the following lab findings would be expected?
options: Low vitamin D, low calcium, high PTH, low phosphate
Low vitamin D, high calcium, high phosphate
Normal vitamin D, low calcium, low PTH
High vitamin D, high calcium, low PTH
explanations: Correct: rickets results from vitamin D deficiency (poor sun exposure, malabsorption), leading to decreased calcium absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH), and PTH-mediated phosphate wasting (low phosphate), causing defective growth plate mineralization.
Vitamin D deficiency causes low, not high, calcium, and phosphate is low (not high) due to PTH-driven renal wasting.
PTH should be elevated (not low) as a compensatory response to hypocalcemia in rickets.
High vitamin D/calcium with low PTH is not consistent with rickets, which involves vitamin D deficiency.
questions.overview: Rickets is defective mineralization of the cartilaginous growth plate in children due to vitamin D or calcium deficiency, causing bowed legs (genu varum), widened epiphyses, rachitic rosary, and craniotabes. Labs classically show low vitamin D, low calcium, low phosphate, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), and elevated bone alkaline phosphatase.

questions.stem: An infant presents with pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and dense bones on x-ray with a "bone-in-bone" appearance. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in carbonic anhydrase type II. What is the underlying defect?
explanations: Defective vitamin D activation causes rickets/osteomalacia, not osteopetrosis.
Osteoblast activity is relatively unopposed (not defective) in osteopetrosis; the defect is in osteoclasts.
Defective collagen cross-linking is not the mechanism described in osteopetrosis.

Correct: osteopetrosis results from defective osteoclast activity (impaired acid secretion due to carbonic anhydrase II mutation in the infantile autosomal recessive form), leading to failure of bone resorption, increased bone density, loss of marrow space (pancytopenia), and extramedullary hematopoiesis (hepatosplenomegaly).
questions.overview: Osteopetrosis results from defective osteoclast bone resorption, causing overgrowth of dense, brittle bone that fills the marrow cavity (pancytopenia, extramedullary hematopoiesis) and compresses cranial nerves. The severe infantile autosomal recessive form is caused by carbonic anhydrase type II mutations (impaired acid secretion by osteoclasts) and may be curable with bone marrow transplant, while a milder autosomal dominant form (Albers-Schönberg disease) involves CLCN7 mutations.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old obese boy presents with groin and thigh pain and a limp that worsens with activity. Hip exam shows limited internal rotation. X-ray reveals displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck, resembling an "ice cream cone." What is the diagnosis?
explanations: DDH presents in infancy with asymmetric skin folds and positive Ortolani/Barlow maneuvers, not in an obese adolescent with the ice cream cone sign.
Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in younger children with hip pain after a viral illness, not associated with the ice cream cone sign.
Osteoid osteoma presents as bone pain (often nocturnal, relieved by NSAIDs/aspirin) with a radiolucent nidus, not epiphyseal slippage.

Correct: SCFE typically occurs in obese adolescents (12-14 years) when pressure on the femoral head causes the epiphysis to shift/slip from the femoral neck, producing groin pain and the classic "ice cream cone sign" on x-ray, with risk of progression to avascular necrosis.

Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in younger children (4-8 years), more common in males, with an initially normal x-ray, not the ice cream cone sign in an obese adolescent.
questions.overview: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) occurs in obese adolescents (12-14 years) when the femoral head epiphysis slips relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, causing groin pain and the "ice cream cone sign" on x-ray, with risk of progression to avascular necrosis. It is distinguished from Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurring in younger children (4-8 years, more common in males).

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the role of osteoprotegerin (OPG) in bone remodeling?
options: OPG is a decoy receptor secreted by osteoblasts that binds RANK-L and inhibits osteoclast activation
OPG is secreted by osteoclasts and stimulates RANK on osteoblasts
OPG directly binds RANK on osteoclasts to activate bone resorption
OPG is a hormone that increases serum calcium independent of RANK-L
explanations: Correct: OPG is produced by osteoblasts and acts as a decoy receptor, binding RANK-L and preventing it from binding RANK on osteoclasts, thereby inhibiting osteoclast activation and bone resorption.
OPG is secreted by osteoblasts, not osteoclasts, and it inhibits (not stimulates) osteoclast activation.
OPG binds RANK-L (not RANK directly) and inhibits, rather than activates, bone resorption.
OPG's mechanism is specifically through blocking the RANK-L/RANK interaction, not acting as an independent calcium-regulating hormone.
questions.overview: Bone turnover is regulated by the RANK/RANK-L/OPG axis: osteoblasts express RANK-L, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to stimulate osteoclast differentiation and activity, while osteoblasts also secrete osteoprotegerin (OPG), a decoy receptor that binds RANK-L and blocks this interaction, inhibiting osteoclasts. Estrogen increases OPG and decreases RANK-L/M-CSF, explaining accelerated bone loss after menopause when estrogen declines.

questions.stem: A patient is started on diltiazem for rate control. Compared with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like diltiazem and verapamil have which of the following properties?
options: Selective action on vascular smooth muscle only, with no cardiac effects
No effect on L-type calcium channels
Higher affinity for cardiac L-type calcium channels, producing greater negative inotropic and chronotropic effects
explanations: Non-dihydropyridines act significantly on cardiac tissue (not just vascular smooth muscle), which is precisely why they are used for rate/rhythm control.
Calcium channel blockers act on L-type (dihydropyridine) receptors on the cell surface, not ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Non-dihydropyridines do block L-type calcium channels; this is their mechanism of action.

Correct: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) have higher affinity for cardiac L-type calcium channels compared with dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine), resulting in decreased contractility (negative inotropy), slowed conduction, and lower heart rate.
questions.overview: Cardiac L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors) mediate calcium influx during phase 2 of the cardiac action potential, triggering calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and contraction. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) have higher cardiac affinity and reduce contractility, conduction velocity, and heart rate, while dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) preferentially act on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with a painful, warm, swollen mass over the diaphysis of the femur, along with low-grade fever and leukocytosis. Blood cultures and tumor aspirate are sterile. X-ray shows a lamellated "onion skin" periosteal reaction. Cytogenetic analysis reveals a translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Correct: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant tumor of undifferentiated neuroectodermal cells occurring in children/adolescents (peak 10-15 years), typically in the diaphysis of long bones, presenting with a painful, warm, swollen mass that can mimic osteomyelitis (fever, leukocytosis) but with sterile cultures; the t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 translocation is diagnostic, and x-ray shows an "onion skin" periosteal reaction.
Chondrosarcoma occurs in older adults, arising from cartilage, and is not associated with t(11;22) or an onion skin periosteal reaction in a child.
Osteosarcoma occurs at the metaphysis with a Codman triangle/sunburst pattern and pleomorphic osteoid-producing cells, not onion skin and small round blue cells with t(11;22).
Osteomyelitis would typically show positive blood cultures/aspirate, unlike the sterile cultures described here.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis presents with bone masses (often skull) and biopsy showing Langerhans cells/eosinophils, not the translocation described.
questions.overview: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant tumor of primitive neuroectodermal (small round blue) cells that occurs in the diaphysis of long bones in children/adolescents (peak 10-15 years), often mimicking osteomyelitis with fever and leukocytosis but sterile cultures. It is characterized by the t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 translocation and an "onion skin" periosteal reaction on imaging.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man sustains a midshaft humeral fracture after a fall. On exam, he has weakness of wrist and finger extension with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand; triceps strength and sensation over the posterior arm are intact. Which nerve is injured, and at what level?
options: Radial nerve, injury above the spiral groove (proximal to triceps branch)
Radial nerve, injury at the spiral groove/midshaft (distal to triceps branch)
explanations: Median nerve injury causes thenar weakness and sensory loss over the thumb-side of the hand, not wrist drop.
Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness, not wrist drop.
Ulnar nerve injury causes weakness of hand intrinsics and sensory loss over the little finger side, not wrist drop.
Injury above the level supplying the triceps (more proximal) would also cause triceps weakness and posterior arm sensory loss, which are preserved in this patient.

Correct: the radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus and is vulnerable at the midshaft; injury at or below the branch to the triceps spares triceps function and posterior arm sensation while causing wrist drop and dorsal hand paresthesia.
questions.overview: The radial nerve travels in the spiral groove adjacent to the humeral shaft and is classically injured by midshaft humerus fractures or compression ("Saturday night palsy," crutches), producing wrist drop, weak finger extension, and dorsal hand sensory loss. Because the triceps branch arises proximally, injuries at or below the spiral groove spare triceps strength and posterior arm sensation.

questions.stem: An older male smoker of Northern European descent presents with painless, progressive difficulty extending his ring and little fingers due to thickening of the palmar fascia. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the thumb-side wrist tendons, causing pain with thumb movement, not painless finger contracture.
Trigger finger is not the mechanism described; the vignette specifically describes palmar fascia thickening, consistent with Dupuytren contracture.
Ganglion cysts are painless fluid-filled masses along tendons/joints (often the dorsal wrist), not fascial thickening causing contracture.

Correct: Dupuytren contracture is fibroblastic proliferation and thickening of the palmar fascia, typically affecting the ring and little fingers, more common in older men of Northern European descent with risk factors including smoking and alcohol use; it presents as a painless, progressive flexion contracture.
questions.overview: Dupuytren contracture is fibroblastic proliferation and thickening of the palmar fascia of unknown etiology, typically affecting the ring and little fingers and causing a painless, progressive flexion contracture. Risk factors include older age, male sex, smoking, alcohol use, and Northern European ancestry; treatment includes collagenase injection, needle aponeurotomy, or fasciectomy.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with progressive pain and swelling of the distal femur near the knee. X-ray shows periosteal elevation with a triangular area of new bone formation and a sunburst pattern of spicules extending into soft tissue. Biopsy shows pleomorphic cells producing irregular osteoid. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Giant cell tumor occurs in the epiphysis with a "soap bubble" appearance and multinucleated giant osteoclast-like cells, not osteoid-producing pleomorphic cells.
Osteochondroma is a benign cartilage-capped bony projection at the metaphysis, not an aggressive osteoid-producing lesion.
Chondrosarcoma occurs in older adults (>50 years), typically in the pelvis/proximal femur/humerus, composed of malignant chondrocytes, not osteoid-producing cells.
Ewing sarcoma occurs in the diaphysis, shows an "onion skin" periosteal reaction, and consists of small round blue cells, not osteoid-producing pleomorphic cells.

Correct: osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone malignancy, typically affecting the metaphysis of long bones (50% around the knee) in adolescents; the Codman triangle (periosteal elevation) and sunburst pattern on x-ray, with biopsy showing pleomorphic osteoblasts producing osteoid, are classic.
questions.overview: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor, occurring in a bimodal distribution (adolescents and older adults with Paget's disease or prior radiation), typically at the metaphysis of long bones around the knee. Classic imaging findings are the Codman triangle and sunburst/sunray periosteal reaction, with histology showing pleomorphic cells producing irregular osteoid; treatment includes neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgical resection.

questions.stem: A patient with prolonged bed rest and habitual leg crossing develops foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral shin. Which nerve is most likely compressed, and at what anatomic site?
options: Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
Tibial nerve at the tarsal tunnel
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
explanations: Sciatic nerve compression by the piriformis causes buttock pain, not this isolated foot drop/sensory pattern.
Femoral nerve compression affects hip flexion/knee extension and anteromedial thigh sensation, not foot drop.
Tibial nerve compression at the tarsal tunnel causes sensory symptoms of the sole of the foot, not foot drop.

Correct: the common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck, where it is vulnerable to compression (prolonged lying, leg crossing, casts), producing foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot/lateral shin.
questions.overview: The common peroneal nerve wraps superficially around the fibular neck, making it susceptible to compression from prolonged bed rest, leg casts, or fibular neck fracture. Injury causes foot drop (weak dorsiflexion), a "steppage gait," and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral shin.

questions.stem: A man grabs a tree branch while falling, causing sudden excessive abduction of his arm. Exam reveals weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles with metacarpophalangeal joint hyperextension and interphalangeal joint flexion ("clawed hand"), while wrist flexion is preserved. Which brachial plexus structure is most likely injured?
explanations: Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the shoulder, not hand findings.
Upper trunk injury produces Erb's palsy with a waiter's tip deformity (weak abduction/elbow flexion), not a clawed hand.
Musculocutaneous nerve injury affects elbow flexion/supination and lateral forearm sensation, not hand intrinsics.
Long thoracic nerve injury causes scapular winging, unrelated to hand findings.

Correct: the lower trunk (C8-T1) gives rise to ulnar and median nerve contributions to the intrinsic hand muscles; wrist flexors are spared because they are supplied by different roots, producing Klumpke palsy with a clawed hand.
questions.overview: Klumpke palsy results from excessive upward traction/abduction of the arm (e.g., catching a branch while falling, or upward force during a difficult delivery), injuring the lower trunk (C8-T1) and thus the ulnar and median nerve contributions to the intrinsic hand muscles. Because forearm wrist flexors are innervated by different nerve roots, they are spared, producing a clawed hand.

questions.stem: A competitive cyclist develops numbness in the little and ring fingers along with weakness of finger abduction/adduction after months of training. Which structure is most likely compressed?
options: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
explanations: Correct: Guyon canal (ulnar canal) syndrome results from repetitive pressure on the ulnar nerve at the wrist (e.g., from bicycle handlebars), causing sensory loss over the little finger side and weakness of the interossei (abduction/adduction).
Radial nerve compression at the spiral groove causes wrist drop, not the sensory/motor pattern described.
Musculocutaneous nerve injury affects elbow flexion and lateral forearm sensation, unrelated to this presentation.
Median nerve compression (carpal tunnel) causes thumb-side sensory loss and thenar weakness, not little/ring finger symptoms.
questions.overview: Guyon canal syndrome is compression of the ulnar nerve at the wrist, classically caused by repetitive pressure from bicycle handlebars or hook of hamate fracture/dislocation. It produces sensory loss over the little finger side of the hand and weakness of the interosseous muscles (finger abduction/adduction) and hypothenar muscles.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman reports numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger that worsens at night. Lightly tapping over the volar wrist reproduces the symptoms. Sensation over the palm is preserved. Which of the following is most likely?
explanations: Radial nerve compression causes wrist/finger extensor weakness (wrist drop) and dorsal hand sensory loss, not this volar sensory pattern.

Correct: carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve entrapment at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum; pregnancy-related edema is a risk factor. Sensory loss involves the lateral 3½ fingers with sparing of the palm because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel; tapping reproduces symptoms (Tinel's sign).
Cubital tunnel syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, causing little/ring finger symptoms, not thumb-side symptoms.
Guyon canal syndrome involves the ulnar nerve, causing sensory loss over the little finger/ulnar side of the hand, not the thumb/index/middle fingers.

Thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the lower trunk/subclavian vessels, causing ulnar-distribution and vascular symptoms throughout the arm, not this discrete median sensory pattern with palm sparing.
questions.overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve entrapment at the wrist beneath the flexor retinaculum, causing sensory loss/paresthesia over the thumb, index, middle, and lateral ring finger with sparing of palm sensation (the palmar cutaneous branch exits proximal to the tunnel). Risk factors include pregnancy, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, and acromegaly; Tinel's and Phalen's signs support the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness, a purple discoloration of the upper eyelids, and scaly erythematous papules over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. Muscle biopsy shows perimysial inflammation with predominant CD4+ T-cells. What is the diagnosis?
explanations: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder without inflammation, muscle damage, weakness, or skin findings, and has normal biopsy/labs.
Polymyositis lacks skin involvement and shows endomysial inflammation with predominant CD8+ T-cells, not the perimysial/CD4+ pattern or skin findings described.

Correct: dermatomyositis presents with proximal muscle weakness plus characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash over the eyelids, Gottron papules over the hand joints), and muscle biopsy shows perimysial inflammation with predominant CD4+ T-cells; it is associated with increased malignancy risk.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes muscle pain/stiffness without true weakness, a normal CK, and no skin findings or muscle biopsy inflammation as described.
questions.overview: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness plus pathognomonic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules), with muscle biopsy showing perimysial inflammation predominated by CD4+ T-cells (versus polymyositis's endomysial CD8+ T-cell pattern). Both show elevated CK and are associated with malignancy (more strongly for dermatomyositis) and are treated with corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand while skateboarding. He has tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox, but the initial wrist x-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step, and what complication is he at risk for if the injury is missed?
options: Immediate surgery; risk of median nerve injury
Immobilize as if fractured and repeat imaging; risk of avascular necrosis
Observation only; risk of Guyon canal syndrome
MRI now; risk of ulnar artery thrombosis
Reassure and discharge; no risk of complication
explanations: Immediate surgery is not first-line, and median nerve injury is not the classic complication of scaphoid fracture (avascular necrosis/nonunion are).

Correct: the scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, classically from a FOOSH injury; snuffbox tenderness with normal initial x-ray warrants immobilization and repeat imaging, since the scaphoid's retrograde blood supply (from the radial artery) makes the proximal pole prone to avascular necrosis and nonunion if untreated.
Guyon canal syndrome involves the ulnar nerve and is unrelated to scaphoid fracture, which risks avascular necrosis/nonunion.
MRI is not the routine next step in this scenario, and ulnar artery thrombosis is not the classic scaphoid fracture complication.
Reassurance is inappropriate; snuffbox tenderness is a classic finding for scaphoid fracture even with normal initial imaging.
questions.overview: The scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone, typically from a FOOSH injury, and presents with anatomic snuffbox tenderness even when initial x-rays are normal, requiring immobilization and repeat imaging. Its retrograde blood supply (distal-to-proximal via the radial artery) makes the proximal pole susceptible to avascular necrosis and nonunion, especially with waist fractures.

questions.stem: A patient who underwent axillary lymph node dissection develops difficulty with overhead arm movements. When asked to push against a wall with outstretched arms, the scapula protrudes abnormally from the back. Which nerve was most likely injured?
explanations: Suprascapular nerve injury affects the supraspinatus/infraspinatus, not the serratus anterior or scapular winging.
Thoracodorsal nerve innervates latissimus dorsi and is not the classic cause of scapular winging described here.
Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the shoulder, not scapular winging.

Correct: the long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the rib cage; it is commonly injured during axillary node dissection or stab wounds, causing winging of the scapula, best demonstrated by pushing against a wall.
questions.overview: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior, which stabilizes the scapula against the rib cage during arm movement. It is vulnerable to injury during axillary lymph node dissection or penetrating trauma, resulting in winging of the scapula, most apparent when the patient pushes an outstretched arm against a wall.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why intermittent, low-dose teriparatide (recombinant PTH) increases bone mass, whereas continuous elevation of PTH causes net bone resorption?
options: Intermittent dosing works only on osteoclasts directly, bypassing osteoblasts
Continuous PTH exposure has no effect on bone
Intermittent dosing favors osteoblast-mediated bone formation, while continuous exposure favors osteoclast-mediated resorption
explanations: PTH receptors are on osteoblasts, not osteoclasts; osteoclasts are activated indirectly via osteoblast signaling (RANK-L), and teriparatide's anabolic effect works through osteoblasts.
Continuous PTH exposure does have an effect on bone—it promotes net bone resorption.
Intermittent dosing stimulates, not inhibits, osteoblast-mediated bone formation.

Correct: PTH has dual effects on bone depending on the pattern of exposure: continuous elevation (as in hyperparathyroidism) favors net bone resorption (increased RANK-L via osteoblasts activating osteoclasts) to raise serum calcium, while intermittent, low-dose administration (teriparatide) favors net osteoblastic bone formation, particularly increasing trabecular bone.
questions.overview: Parathyroid hormone has dose- and timing-dependent effects on bone: continuous elevation (chronic hyperparathyroidism) promotes net bone resorption by increasing osteoblast-derived RANK-L, while intermittent low-dose administration (teriparatide) preferentially stimulates osteoblastic bone formation, especially trabecular bone, making it a unique anabolic osteoporosis therapy given via daily subcutaneous injection.

questions.stem: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve, which innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, classically produces which finding while walking?
explanations: Foot drop results from common peroneal nerve injury, not superior gluteal nerve injury.
Correct: superior gluteal nerve injury weakens the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus), causing the pelvis to drop on the contralateral side during single-leg stance (Trendelenburg sign).
Waiter's tip deformity results from upper trunk (C5-C6) brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy).
Scapular winging results from long thoracic nerve injury affecting the serratus anterior.
questions.overview: The superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1) is a pure motor nerve innervating the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae; it can be injured by intramuscular injections placed too medially. Injury causes weak hip abduction and a Trendelenburg gait, with the pelvis dropping on the side contralateral to the lesion when standing on the affected leg.

questions.stem: A new mother who frequently lifts her infant using her thumbs develops pain at the radial styloid, worsened by thumb movement. Which physical exam maneuver would most likely be positive?
explanations: Correct: De Quervain tenosynovitis involves thickening of tendons (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis) in the first dorsal wrist compartment, often from repetitive thumb use; the Finkelstein test (thumb flexion with ulnar deviation of the wrist) reproduces pain at the radial styloid.
McMurray test assesses for meniscal tears of the knee, unrelated to the wrist/thumb.
Phalen maneuver is used to assess for carpal tunnel syndrome, not De Quervain tenosynovitis.
Tinel's sign is used to assess for carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve), not De Quervain tenosynovitis.
questions.overview: De Quervain tenosynovitis is inflammatory thickening of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons within the first dorsal wrist compartment, typically caused by repetitive thumb/wrist overuse (e.g., lifting an infant, texting). It presents with pain and tenderness at the radial styloid, confirmed by a positive Finkelstein test, and is treated with NSAIDs, splinting, or steroid injection.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most characteristic of a proximal tibial nerve lesion?
options: Loss of dorsiflexion and foot drop
Loss of plantar flexion and toe flexion
explanations: Loss of dorsiflexion/foot drop is caused by common peroneal nerve injury, not tibial nerve injury.
Loss of knee extension is caused by femoral nerve injury.
Loss of hip abduction is caused by superior gluteal nerve injury.
Correct: the tibial nerve innervates the posterior leg muscles responsible for plantar flexion, toe flexion, and inversion; proximal lesions cause inability to stand on toes.
questions.overview: The tibial nerve courses down the posterior leg, innervating muscles responsible for plantar flexion, toe flexion, and inversion, then passes under the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel to supply sensation to the heel/sole. Proximal lesions (e.g., large Baker's cyst) cause motor loss (can't stand on toes), while distal lesions (tarsal tunnel syndrome) cause predominantly sensory symptoms of the sole.

questions.stem: Which joint distribution is most characteristic of osteoarthritis, distinguishing it from rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Symmetric involvement of all finger joints including MCP
MCP and wrist joints, sparing the DIP joints
Exclusively large weight-bearing joints, never the hands
DIP and PIP joints, sparing the MCP joints
explanations: Symmetric involvement of all finger joints including MCP is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis.
MCP joint involvement is more characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis.
Osteoarthritis commonly affects the hands (DIP/PIP/CMC) in addition to weight-bearing joints like the knee and hip.
Correct: osteoarthritis of the hand classically involves the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes), and first CMC joint, sparing the MCP joints.
questions.overview: Osteoarthritis is a non-inflammatory, degenerative joint disease from cartilage breakdown, characteristically involving the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes), and first CMC joint while sparing the MCP joints—a pattern that helps distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis, which favors MCP and wrist joints. Classic x-ray findings include joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term oral alendronate for osteoporosis develops thigh pain, and imaging reveals a transverse fracture of the femoral diaphysis below the lesser trochanter with minimal trauma. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Atypical femur fracture, a rare complication of bisphosphonate therapy
Expected fracture pattern unrelated to medication
explanations: Bisphosphonates do not cause hypercalcemia; they reduce bone resorption and are sometimes used to treat hypercalcemia.

Correct: atypical femur fractures are a rare but serious complication of long-term bisphosphonate therapy, occurring in the subtrochanteric/diaphyseal region with minimal or no trauma, distinct from typical osteoporotic hip fractures (femoral neck/intracapsular/trochanteric).
Bisphosphonates do not cause osteomalacia; they inhibit osteoclasts and are used to treat bone disorders, not induce mineralization defects.
This fracture pattern (diaphyseal, minimal trauma) is atypical and specifically associated with bisphosphonate use, not an expected or unrelated fracture pattern.
questions.overview: Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate, zoledronate) are first-line osteoporosis therapy that bind bone hydroxyapatite and are taken up by osteoclasts, inhibiting their activity and reducing bone resorption. Rare but serious long-term complications include atypical (subtrochanteric/diaphyseal) femur fractures with minimal trauma and osteonecrosis of the jaw.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered vaginally after a difficult delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia holds the affected arm adducted and internally rotated at the side, with the forearm extended and pronated ("waiter's tip" posture). Which brachial plexus structure is most likely injured?
explanations: Lower trunk (C8-T1) injury causes Klumpke palsy with a clawed hand from intrinsic hand muscle weakness, not the waiter's tip posture.
The lumbar plexus (L4-S1 region) supplies the lower limb (e.g., superior gluteal nerve territory) and is unrelated to an upper extremity birth injury.
T12-L1 forms the iliohypogastric nerve of the lumbar plexus, supplying the abdominal wall/suprapubic skin, unrelated to brachial plexus birth injury.

Correct: Erb's palsy results from excessive stretching of the neck-shoulder angle (e.g., shoulder dystocia), damaging the upper trunk (C5-C6) and thus the axillary, musculocutaneous, and suprascapular nerves, producing the "waiter's tip" deformity.
The sacral plexus (L5-S2, sciatic/inferior gluteal nerve territory) supplies the lower limb and is unrelated to this presentation.
questions.overview: Erb's palsy (upper trunk, C5-C6) results from excessive stretching of the neck-shoulder angle, classically from shoulder dystocia during birth or trauma in adults. Loss of axillary (deltoid), musculocutaneous (biceps), and suprascapular (infraspinatus) nerve function produces the "waiter's tip" posture: arm adducted, internally rotated, extended, and pronated.
